learning: Iteration 3 combined y = 0.06 with ki 0.3; line loss returned and max_error did not move, so neither is supported. Wider wheel_track lowers yaw per unit of wheel difference, so the Builder's turning-authority reasoning needs checking against this race's max_error and oscillation.
notes: Builder's geometry (16 mm, x ±0.05, y 0.04, wheel_track 0.15) with the iteration-2 controller, scaled for the wider track: kp 4.4 keeps yaw gain per PWM difference equal to the best design. ki reverted to 0 because iteration 3's ki was confounded with the y change.
rationale: Iteration 2 is the best-scoring controller and geometry pairing (26.99): 16 mm footprints at x = ±0.05 m, y = 0.04 m, kp 3.5, ki 0, kd 0.05, with zero line loss on oval and slalom. Iteration 3 moved y to 0.06 and added ki 0.3 together, so the two changes are confounded. It scored lower (26.62), line loss returned on s-bend and slalom, and max_error stayed at 0.061 m, so I revert both to iteration 2 values. The Builder's geometry sets wheel_track to 0.15 m, and the Builder's proposal and rationale attribute this to more turning authority. The physics works the other way: yaw rate is the wheel-speed difference divided by wheel_track, so a wider track gives less yaw per unit of PWM difference. To keep the effective steering gain equal to the best design, I scale kp by 0.15/0.12, giving 3.5 x 1.25 = 4.4. This isolates the wheel-track test: any change in max_error then reflects the track's effect on dynamics rather than a weaker steering loop. ki stays at 0 and kd at 0.05, with base_speed 1.6 and last_direction recovery unchanged. Expected result is line loss at zero and max_error near 0.061 m. A drop below about 0.058 m would support the Builder's hypothesis, but I make no prediction of the score.
